'''Snowshill Manor''' is a [[National Trust]] property located in the village of [[Snowshill]], [[Gloucestershire]], [[United Kingdom]]. It is a sixteenth-century country house, best known for its twentieth-century owner, [[Charles Paget Wade]], an eccentric who amassed an enormous collection of objects that interested him. He gave the property to the National Trust in 1951, and his collection is still housed there.

== Manor house ==
The property is a typical [[Cotswolds|Cotswold]] [[manor house]],<ref name="nationaltrust" /> made from local stone; the main part of the house dates from the 16th century. It is a Grade II* [[listed building]], having been so designated since 4 July 1960. Also listed are the brewhouse, the dovecote, some of the garden buildings, the wall and gate-piers, and the group of four Manor Cottages.<ref name=BLB/>

==History==
<ref name="NatTrust">{{cite book |last1=Freund |first1=Paul |title=Snowshill Manor and Garden |date=2018 |publisher=The National Trust |isbn=978-1-84359-358-4}}</ref> Snowshill Manor was given to [[Winchcombe Abbey]] in 821 by King [[Coenwulf]] of Mercia. Two hundred and sixty four years later, the village and Manor were listed in the [[Domesday Book]] of 1086 as ''Snawesille, property of the Abbey of Saint Mary of Winchcombe''.<ref>{{cite web |title=Place name: Snowshill, Gloucestershire Folio: 165v Great Domesday Book |url=http://discovery.nationalarchives.gov.uk/details/r/D7305713 |website=The National Archives' catalogue |publisher=The National Archives}}</ref> The Manor remained the property of the Abbey until the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] in 1539<ref name="mysterious" /> when it was confiscated by [[Henry VIII of England|King Henry VIII]], who included the Manor in his dowry to his last queen, [[Catherine Parr]], in 1543.

The earliest surviving part of the Manor, the rooms named and now known as ''Dragon, Nadir, Ann's, Music'' and ''Seraphim'' by [[Charles Paget Wade]], was built around 1550 and it is probable that this section of the Manor was joined to a contemporaneous building to the south, which was later demolished. In the 1600s the Manor was again extended southwards and attic rooms added. In the early part of the 18th century the house was owned by one William Sambach, who added extra rooms on the south-west corner in about 1720. He also added a new main door in the south front, placing the Sambach coat of arms in the pediment above it, which is now the main entrance to the house. After several further changes of owner, John Small of Clapham took over the property, being the first of a series of absentee landlords: for the next 150 years the house was occupied by tenant farmers, until its purchase in 1919 by [[Charles Paget Wade]].<ref name="NatTrust" />

Wade was an [[architecture|architect]], [[Arts and Crafts Movement|artist-craftsman]], collector, [[poetry|poet]] and heir to the family fortune. He restored the property, living in the small cottage in the garden and using the Manor house as a home for his collection of objects. By the time of his death he had amassed over 22,000 objects.
He gave the property and the contents of this collection to the National Trust in 1951.<ref name=BLB>{{cite web |url=http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-134827-snowshill-manor-snowshill-gloucestershir#.V8Hfw63GD6g |title=Snowshill Manor, Snowshill |publisher=British Listed Buildings |accessdate=27 August 2016}}</ref>

== Collections ==
The house contains an eclectic collection of thousands of objects, gathered over the years by [[Charles Paget Wade]], whose motto was "Let nothing perish". The collection includes toys, [[Samurai armour]], musical instruments, and clocks.<ref name="nationaltrust" /> Today, the main attraction of the house is perhaps the display of Wade's collection. From 1900 until 1951, when he gave the Manor to the National Trust, Wade amassed an enormous and eclectic collection of objects reflecting his interest in [[Artisan|craftsmanship]]. The objects in the collection include 26 suits of [[Japan]]ese [[samurai]] [[armour]] dating from the 17th and 19th centuries, [[bicycle]]s, [[toy]]s, [[musical instrument]]s, and more.<ref name=Child/>

== Priest's House ==
Wade was an eccentric man and lived in the Priest's House while housing his collection in the manor. It is said to be haunted by a monk, and by the ghost of a young woman forced in 1604 to marry against her will in one of the upstairs rooms.<ref name=Child>{{cite book|author=Mark Child|title=The Windrush Valley|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=15CIAwAAQBAJ&pg=PT17 |year=2013 |publisher=Amberley Publishing Limited |isbn=978-1-4456-3161-5 |page=17}}</ref>

== Garden ==
The garden at Snowshill was laid out by Wade, in collaboration with [[Arts and Crafts movement]] architect, M. H. [[Baillie Scott]], between 1920 and 1923. Their elaborate layout resembles a series of outside rooms seen as an extension to the house. Features include terraces and ponds, and the gardens demonstrate Wade's fascination with colours and scents.<ref name=Olson>{{cite book|author1=Donald Olson|author2=Stephen Brewer|author3=Donald Strachan|author4=Barry Shelby|title=Frommer's Great Britain Day by Day|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cxAVBF_pdNwC&pg=PA311 |year=2012 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-0-470-64869-8 |page=311}}</ref> As well as formal beds, the gardens include an ancient dovecote, a model village, kitchen garden, orchards and small fields with sheep.<ref name="nationaltrust" />

=== Wolf's Cove model village ===
This [[Miniature park|model village]] was originally built by Wade, in 1907, in the garden of his Lodgings in Hampstead. It was originally called 'Fladbury', but renamed to Wolf's Cove when he moved and expanded it in the late 1920's. It is a 1/2" scale model of a Cornish fishing village, centred round a harbour, with pubs, cottages and a railway.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Foster |first1=Camilla |title=Snowshill Manor and Garden will exhibit famous model village |url=https://www.wiltsglosstandard.co.uk/news/23399862.snowshill-manor-garden-will-exhibit-famous-model-village/ |access-date=5 March 2026 |work=Wilts and Gloucestershire Standard |date=20 March 2023}}</ref>

1423790.title: Woodchester
1423790.extract:
Woodchester is a Gloucestershire village in the Nailsworth (or Woodchester) Valley, a valley in the South Cotswolds in England, running southwards from Stroud along the A46 road to Nailsworth. The parish population taken at the 2011 census was 1,206.
Woodchester is approximately at the midpoint between Stroud and Nailsworth, about two miles south of Stroud. It is divided into North and South Woodchester, with a side valley between the two settlements. There are pubs in both North and South (The Royal Oak in North and The Ram in South) and a post office with a shop in North Woodchester. There was a post office (called Woodchester) in South Woodchester but it closed, along with the shop, in June 2008. Woodchester is notable as the location of Woodchester Roman Villa. The village's parish church of St Mary's was designed by Samuel Sanders Teulon.
The nearby Woodchester Mansion is regularly open to the public and stands in a landscaped valley. This valley is now owned by the National Trust and is open daily. There are three waymarked walks. The car park is at Nympsfield near Coaley Peak, not at Woodchester as some visitors suppose.
Education is provided by the Woodchester Endowed C of E Primary School under Headteacher Mrs Pennington, which serves around 135 pupils. Following the Ofsted inspection in 2018, the school was rated Outstanding, point four on a four-point scale. The school has secured the Healthy Schools award.
The former Convent of Poor Clares was home to nuns of the Poor Clares order from 1850 to 2011.

Woodchester is notable as the location of [[Woodchester Roman Villa]].<ref>Graham Thomas (2000) ''The Romans at Woodchester'' [http://www.grahamthomas.com/history4.html Orpheus Mosaic at Woodchester]</ref> The village's parish church of St Mary's was designed by [[Samuel Sanders Teulon]].

'''May Hill''' is a prominent English hill between [[Gloucester]] and [[Ross-on-Wye]]. Its [[summit]], on the western edge of [[Gloucestershire]] and its northern slopes in [[Herefordshire]], is distinguishable by a clump of trees on its summit, which forms an official [[biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest|Site of Special Scientific Interest]].<ref name=NationalTrustMayHill>{{Cite web |title=May Hill – Visitor Information |publisher=[[National Trust]] |url=http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-mayhill |access-date=22 June 2012 |archive-date=16 January 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120116033603/http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/main/w-mayhill |url-status=live}}</ref> It is reached by three public footpaths, two as parts of the [[Gloucestershire Way]] and [[Wysis Way]].<ref name=MayHillcountrysidewalk>{{Cite web |title=May Hill countryside walk |publisher=[[National Trust]] |url= http://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/servlet/pdf/1/540852/Trail/Walking/May_Hill_countryside_walk,_Gloucestershire.pdf |access-date=22 June 2012}}</ref>

==Toponymy==
There is an unverified story that May Hill was named after a certain Captain May who used it as a landmark when navigating the Severn estuary, but documents from a couple of hundred years ago relate that the hill was known as Yartleton Hill and was renamed because of the [[May Day]] events held there.<ref name=LonghopeVillage>{{Cite web |title=May Hill |publisher=The Longhope Village Website |url=http://www.longhopevillage.co.uk/history/hills.asp |access-date=22 June 2012 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183355/http://www.longhopevillage.co.uk/History/MayHill/ |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bullock |first=Arthur |title=Gloucestershire Between the Wars: A Memoir |publisher=The History Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-7524-4793-3}} Page 39.
</ref> Each May Day, [[morris dance]]rs dance in the new dawn on the top of May Hill and hundreds of observers join in the celebration.<ref name=MayHillWyenot/> A ceremony on May Day morning has been carried out for several centuries; originally it included a mock battle between youths.<ref name=LonghopeVillage/>

==Geography==
[[File:Severn from May Hill.jpg|thumb|right|The Severn from May Hill]]
May Hill forms part of a low range of hills separating the [[River Severn]] from the [[River Wye]]. The summit is {{convert|296|m|ft|0}} above sea level. Among the trees there are several benches from which the views in all directions can be seen. They include views to the [[Wales-England border|Welsh borders]], and the lower reaches of the [[River Severn]], bypassed for shipping by the [[Gloucester and Sharpness Canal]].<ref name=MayHillWyenot>{{Cite web |title=May Hill |publisher=wyenot.com |url=http://www.wyenot.com/mayhill.htm |access-date=22 June 2012 |archive-date=23 November 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191123112958/http://www.wyenot.com/mayhill.htm |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Geology==
May Hill is formed of [[sandstone]]s and siltstones known as the May Hill sandstone, consisting of the Huntley Hill and Yartleton formations. These rocks date from the [[Llandovery epoch|Early Silurian]] period and are formed into a [[Dome (geology)|dome]], cut through by several faults. The most significant of these is the Blaisdon Fault, which forms the eastern boundary of May Hill and separates it from the younger rocks of the [[Severn Vale]].<ref name=GloucestershireGeologyTrust>{{Cite web |title=Huntley Quarry Geology Reserve |publisher=Gloucestershire Geology Trust |url=http://www.glosgeotrust.org.uk/huntleyquarry.shtml |access-date=22 June 2012 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183341/http://www.glosgeotrust.org.uk/huntleyquarry.shtml |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Ecology and SSSI status==

The summit of May Hill ({{gbmapping|SO695214}}) is a {{convert|32.6|ha|adj=on}} [[biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in Gloucestershire, [[SSSI notification|notified]] in 1954.<ref name="NE citation">{{Cite web |url=http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/Special/sssi/sssi_details.cfm?sssi_id=1001791 |publisher=Natural England |title=SSSI information on citation, map and unit details |access-date=7 July 2012 |archive-date=2 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131002021429/http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/Special/sssi/sssi_details.cfm?sssi_id=1001791 |url-status=live}}</ref><ref>[http://www.fdean.gov.uk/nqcontent.cfm?a_id=6464&tt=graphic Forest of Dean District Local Plan Review, adopted November 2005, Appendix D 'Nature Conservation Site Designations Within the Forest of Dean District', Sites of Special Scientific Interest] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029192727/http://www.fdean.gov.uk/nqcontent.cfm?a_id=6464&tt=graphic |date=29 October 2013}}</ref>

May Hill is listed in the Forest of Dean Local Plan Review as a Key Wildlife Site (KWS).<ref>[http://www.fdean.gov.uk/nqcontent.cfm?a_id=6464&tt=graphic Forest of Dean District Local Plan Review, adopted November 2005, Appendix D 'Nature Conservation Site Designations Within the Forest of Dean District', Key Wildlife Sites] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029192727/http://www.fdean.gov.uk/nqcontent.cfm?a_id=6464&tt=graphic |date=29 October 2013}}</ref>

Much of May Hill is wooded, both [[coniferous]] and [[deciduous]], but the summit area is [[grassland]] and [[heath (habitat)|heath]], with a small amount of [[Calluna|heather]] and [[gorse]]. The immediate summit is topped with mature [[Pinus nigra|Corsican pines]], planted in 1887 to mark [[Queen Victoria]]'s [[Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria|Golden Jubilee]]. One very old Scots Pine is a generation older, but which regrettably suffered badly in an ice storm in early 2012.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/may-hill#Overview|title = May Hill}}</ref> The trees make May Hill an identifiable landmark from many miles away. The younger trees were planted to mark Queen Elizabeth's Silver Jubilee. Early maps and accounts show a clump of trees on the top before these plantings.<ref name=LonghopeVillage/> Birds to be seen on the hill include [[meadow pipit]], [[tree pipit]],<ref name=MayHillcountrysidewalk/> [[common redstart]] and [[Common raven|raven]], whilst the woods below have a good population of [[Eurasian woodcock|woodcock]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Newent Woods area |url=https://glosnats.org/newent-woods-area/ |publisher=Gloucestershire Naturalists Society |access-date=21 August 2020 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183318/https://glosnats.org/newent-woods-area/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

==History==
The hill includes a circular trench 100 metres in diameter, thought to be an [[Iron Age]] earthwork, surrounding a mound that is probably a [[round barrow]].<ref name="LonghopeVillage" />

There are records of a clump of trees on the summit of May Hill dating back to the later 18th century. The hill was [[Inclosure Acts|enclosed]] by an Act of Parliament in 1873. The dwindling clump was replenished in time for the [[Golden Jubilee of Queen Victoria]] in 1887, when most of the trees that give the hill its distinctive character today were planted.<ref name=LonghopeVillage/><ref>{{Cite book |last=Bullock |first=Arthur |title=Gloucestershire Between the Wars: A Memoir |publisher=The History Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-7524-4793-3}} Pages 22-24.</ref>

An area of 30 ha of the hill passed into the care of the [[National Trust]] in 1935,<ref name=LonghopeVillage/><ref name=NationalTrustMayHill/> although the summit has remained vested with [[Longhope]] Parish Council and registered as a [[Village green#Town and village greens|village green]].

There was further replenishment of the trees in 1977 for the [[Silver Jubilee of Elizabeth II]]. A plaque on the summit commemorating this reads:
{{blockquote|This plaque was erected by the parishes of Longhope & Newent as a tribute to a gracious and beloved monarch. God Save the Queen.<ref name=MayHillWyenot/>}}

The site boundary was amended in 1983.<ref name="NE citation"/>

May Hill used to have a football club, whose biggest honour was winning the George Sandoe Cup in the 1950s. The village no longer has a football team, the closest being [[Longhope#Longhope_Football_Club|Longhope Football Club]] in the neighbouring village.

==May Hill in cultural life==
May Hill is associated with the poets [[Edward Thomas (poet)|Edward Thomas]] and [[Robert Frost]]. [[John Masefield]] describes May Hill in his poem "[[The Everlasting Mercy]]".<ref name=MayHillForestofDean>{{Cite web |title=May Hill Forest of Dean website |publisher=Forest of Dean Tourist Information Official Site |url=http://www.visitforestofdean.co.uk/thedms.aspx?dms=13&nearby=1&GroupId=2&venue=1301234 |access-date=18 December 2011 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183324/http://www.wyedeantourism.co.uk/discover/thingstodo/i-4391-May_Hill |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Ivor Gurney]] eulogised "May Hill that Gloucester dwellers 'gainst every sunset see." Composer [[Gerald Finzi]]'s ashes were scattered on the top in 1973.<ref>McVeagh, Diana M. ''Gerald Finzi: His Life and Music'' (Woodbridge, Suffolk: Boydell Press, 2005), p. 251.</ref> One of the benches on the summit is dedicated to the [[Forest of Dean]] chronicler, [[Winifred Foley]], and her husband, who had moved to the nearby village of [[Cliffords Mesne]] in the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=May Hill |url=http://www.wyedeantourism.co.uk/discover/all/t-3597%7C/i-4391-May_Hill |publisher=Forest of Dean and Wye Valley |access-date=21 August 2020 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183357/http://www.wyedeantourism.co.uk/discover/all/t-3597%7C/i-4391-May_Hill |url-status=usurped}}</ref> A book of paintings and drawings of May Hill has been published by the artist Valerie McLean.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://valeriemclean.com/products-page/ |title=May Hill Book |date=30 March 2010 |access-date=24 February 2019 |archive-date=21 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200821183326/http://valeriemclean.com/products-page/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

'''Hidcote Manor Garden''' is a garden in the United Kingdom, located at the village of [[Hidcote Bartrim]], near [[Chipping Campden]], [[Gloucestershire]]. It is one of the best-known and most influential [[Arts and Crafts movement|Arts and Crafts]] gardens in Britain, with its linked "[[garden room]]s" of hedges, rare trees, shrubs and [[herbaceous border]]s. Created by [[Lawrence Waterbury Johnston|Lawrence Johnston]], it is owned by the [[National Trust]] and is open to the public.

== History ==
The Americans, [[Lawrence Waterbury Johnston|Lawrence Johnston]] and his mother, settled in Britain about 1900, and Lawrence immediately became a British citizen and fought in the [[British Army]] during the [[Boer war]]. In 1907 Johnston's mother, Mrs Gertrude Winthrop (she had re-married), purchased the Hidcote Manor Estate. It was situated in a part of Britain with strong connections to the then-burgeoning [[Arts and Crafts movement]] and an Anglicized American artistic expatriate community centred nearby at [[Broadway, Worcestershire]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Hidcote: The Making of a Garden|first=Ethne|last=Clarke|date=1989|pages=30–1}}</ref>

Johnston soon became interested in turning the fields around the house into a [[Garden design|garden]]. In 1907 he began to lay out the key features of the garden.<ref>{{cite book|title=Hidcote|last=Clarke|page=43}}</ref> There are no records to show how many gardeners were employed,<ref>{{cite book|title=Lawrence Johnston: Creator of Hidcote|first=Graham S.|last=Pearson|date=2013|page=75}}</ref> but they were directly managed by Lawrence. It was only in 1922, when the garden was essentially complete, that Frank Adams arrived at Hidcote from [[Windsor Castle]] to act as head gardener.<ref>{{cite book|title=Lawrence Johnston|last=Pearson|page=125}}</ref>

The garden became a strong influence on the designer [[Phyllis Reiss]] who lived nearby in Dowdeswell Manor. She and her husband bought [[Tintinhull Garden]] in Somerset in 1933 so that they could have their own gardens based on the Hidcote Manor style.<ref>{{Cite web|title=TINTINHULL HOUSE, Tintinhull - 1001156 {{!}} Historic England|url=https://historicengland.org.uk/listing/the-list/list-entry/1001156|access-date=2021-04-02|website=historicengland.org.uk|language=en}}</ref>

After World War II Johnston spent most of his time at [[Jardin Serre de la Madone]], his garden in the south of France; and in 1947 he entrusted Hidcote to the National Trust.<ref>{{cite web|url= https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2023/apr/16/walking-through-beauty-in-hidden-gardens-of-hidcote|first=John-Paul|last=Flintoff|title=Walking through beauty in hidden gardens of Hidcote|work=The Guardian|date=16 April 2023|access-date=17 April 2023}}</ref>

The style of the garden has been widely imitated. In 2007 a temporary garden designed by [[Chris Beardshaw]] that drew inspiration from Johnson's Hidcote was constructed at the [[Chelsea Flower Show]] in London.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Chris Beardshaw Garden Celebrating a 100 years of Hidcote Manor Garden {{!}} RHS Chelsea Flower Show 22 May to 26 May 2007 - The Gardening Website |url=https://www.thegardeningwebsite.co.uk/listing/the-chris-beardshaw-garden-celebrating-a-100-years-of-hidcote-manor-garden/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231205135409/https://www.thegardeningwebsite.co.uk/listing/the-chris-beardshaw-garden-celebrating-a-100-years-of-hidcote-manor-garden/ |archive-date=2023-12-05 |access-date=2025-06-07 |website=www.thegardeningwebsite.co.uk |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Character of Hidcote garden ==
[[File:Hidcote7.png|thumb|The Old Garden]]
[[File:Hidcote Manor Garden 02.jpg|thumb|Avenue to gate]]
[[File:Hidcote04.jpg|thumb|White garden]]
Lawrence Johnston was influenced in creating his garden at Hidcote by the work of [[Alfred Parsons (artist)|Alfred Parsons]] and [[Gertrude Jekyll]], who were designing gardens of hardy plants contained within sequences of outdoor "[[garden room]]s". The theme was in the air: [[Vita Sackville-West]] and [[Harold Nicolson]]'s [[Sissinghurst Castle Garden]] was laid out as a sequence of such spaces, without, it seems, direct connection with the reclusive and shy Major Johnston. Hidcote's outdoor "rooms" have various characters and themes, achieved by the use of box [[hedge (barrier)|hedge]]s, [[hornbeam]] and [[taxus|yew]], and stone walls. These rooms, such as the 'White Garden' and '[[Fuchsia]] Garden' are linked, some by vistas, and furnished with [[topiary|topiaries]]. Some have ponds and [[fountain]]s, and all are planted with flowers in bedding schemes. They surround the 17th century [[manor house]], and there are a number of outhouses and a [[kitchen garden]].{{Cn|date=July 2022}}

Johnston's care in selecting the best plants is reflected in the narrow-leaved lavender, [[Lavandula angustifolia]] 'Hidcote', in the [[Penstemon]] 'Hidcote Pink' and in the hybrid [[Hypericum]] 'Hidcote Gold', acclaimed as the finest hardy [[St John's Wort]], [[Alice Margaret Coats|Alice Coats]] records.<ref>Coats, ''Garden Shrubs and Their Histories'' (1964) 1992, s.v. 'Hypericum'</ref>

4933798.title: Horton Court
4933798.extract:
Horton Court is a stone-built 16th century manor house in Horton, near Chipping Sodbury, South Gloucestershire, England. It is a grade I listed building.
Originally a Norman manor, the current house was built in about 1521 by Rev. William Knight (d. 1547), Prothonotary to the Holy See, and later Bishop of Bath and Wells. It retains the 12th-century Norman hall, and displays some of the earliest Renaissance decorative motifs used in England. Within the grounds is a grade I listed ambulatory, built for William Knight around 1527–29.
It has been owned by the National Trust since 1949. As of 2021, it is available for holiday lets.
The parish church of St James the Elder is next door.

It is a grade I [[listed building]].{{NHLE |num=1114992 |desc=Horton Court |accessdate=9 August 2014}} Originally a Norman manor, the current house was built in about 1521 by [[William Knight (royal servant)|Rev. William Knight]] (d. 1547), Prothonotary to the Holy See, and later [[Bishop of Bath and Wells]]. It retains the 12th-century [[Norman architecture|Norman]] [[great hall|hall]], and displays some of the earliest [[Renaissance]] decorative motifs used in England. Within the grounds is a grade I listed [[ambulatory]], built for William Knight around 1527–29.{{NHLE |num=1321166| desc=Ambulatory 20 yards South West of Horton Court |accessdate=5 July 2015}} It has been owned by the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] since 1949. As of 2021, it is available for holiday lets.{{cite web |title=Horton Court |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/horton-court-south-gloucestershire |website=National Trust |access-date=25 January 2022 |language=en |archive-date=25 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220125120439/https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/holidays/horton-court-south-gloucestershire |url-status=live }} The parish church of [[St James the Elder, Horton|St James the Elder]] is next door. ==History== ===See of Sarum=== Early in the 12th century Hubert de Rye donated the manor to the [[See of Salisbury|See of Sarum]], which used the revenues to endow a [[prebend]]. An early Hubert of RyesKeats-Rohan ''Domesday Descendants'' p. 194 is known in legend as the loyal vassal who saved the life of [[William the Conqueror]] in his flight from [[Valognes]] during a revolt in 1047.Douglas ''William the Conqueror'' p. 48 and footnote 8 He was the father of [[Eudo Dapifer]]. A man by the same name in 1164 donated the church of [[Aslackby Preceptory|Aslackby]], Lincolnshire, to the [[Knights Templar]]. The first known holder of the prebend was [[Robert de Bello Fago|Robert de Beaufeu]], around 1150. It is believed he was the builder of the [[Norman architecture|Norman]] [[great hall]], which still survives as the core of the present 16th-century house built by [[William Knight (bishop)|Rev. William Knight]] (1476–1547), a prebendary from 1517. Knight attended [[Oxford University]] and [[Ferrara University]], Italy and travelled to Italy on many occasions on diplomatic missions for [[Henry VIII of England|King Henry VIII]] (1509–1547). He attended the king at the [[Field of the Cloth of Gold]] in 1521, and in 1527 negotiated with the Pope over Henry's divorce from [[Catherine of Aragon]]. He was [[Bishop of Bath and Wells]] from 1541 until his death in 1547. During his travels he witnessed the art of the Italian [[Renaissance]]. He incorporated some of the motifs he had seen abroad into the new house he built in about 1521 at Horton around the Norman hall, and the house is thus one of the earliest English buildings, comparable to [[Sutton Place, Surrey|Sutton Place]], Surrey, and [[Hampton Court]], to show Renaissance design features, most notably in the [[grotesque]] jambs of the front door.Kingsley, Nicholas. ''The Country Houses of Gloucestershire'', Vol.1, 1500-1660, Cheltenham, 1989, pp.109-111, Horton Court His armorials can be seen above the front door and over the entrance hall fireplace, and consist of two [[addorsed]] bird's necks and heads emerging from a demi-sun. The supporters are two grotesque mermaids. The crest, which surmounts the escutcheon directly, consists of a [[prothonotary]]'s hat, which is similar to that of a [[Cardinal (Catholicism)|cardinal]], but is black with three rows of tassels in place of five.National Trust pamphlet, undated, c. 1960s The detached Italianate [[ambulatory]] or [[loggia]] built by Knight survives. ===Paston=== [[File:WilliamPastonByThomasHudson.png|thumb|200px|William Paston Esq. Of Horton com. Gloucester. Died 1769. Painted by [[Thomas Hudson (painter)|Thomas Hudson]] (1701-1779). At [[Coughton Court]], Warwickshire, property of the National Trust, NTPL ref no: 58001]] Following the [[Dissolution of the Monasteries]] Horton became crown property in 1550, and [[Edward VI of England|King Edward VI]] (1547–1553) granted it first to his uncle [[Protector Somerset]] and then in 1550 after his fall to Sir Edward Paston, the younger son of Sir John Paston the Younger (d.1504), by [[Margery Brews]], daughter of Sir Thomas Brews,He had an elder brother also called Sir John Paston (1442-1479), who left no descendants who was knighted at the [[Battle of Stoke]] in 1487. Sir John's father John Paston (1421–1466), MP for Norfolk in 1460 and 1461, wrote the famous [[Paston Letters]]. Horton seems to be an ancestor of Sir Edward Paston (1550–1630), the second son (by Agnes Leigh, daughter of Sir John Leigh of [[Addington, London|Addington]], Surrey and Stockwell) of Sir Thomas Paston, a [[Gentleman of the Privy Chamber]], who in turn was the youngest nephew of Sir Edward Paston, the original grantee in 1550. Sir Thomas Paston's eldest brother Erasmus Paston (1502–1540) was the ancestor of [[Paston baronets|Sir William Paston, 1st Baronet]] (c. 1610–1663), who was created a baronet in 1642, and whose son was [[Robert Paston, 1st Earl of Yarmouth]] (1631–1683). Sir Edward (d.1630), was a godson of King Edward VI. His [[baroque]] mural monument can be seen in [[Blofield]] Church, Norfolk, 4 miles east of [[Norwich]]. He built Appleton Hall, West Newton, Norfolk, where the family lived for several generations until a fire destroyed the house in 1767. They then moved to Horton Court in Gloucestershire.Blomefield, Francis. ''An Essay Towards a Topographical History of the County of Norfolk'', Vol.8, pp.328-332, Appleton Appleton Hall was later rebuilt and became part of the royal [[Sandringham House|Sandringham Estate]], where it was used as a guest house for royal visitors. It became dilapidated during [[World War II]] and was demolished in 1984. ====Paston family monuments==== A monument in the neighbouring Parish Church of St James the Elder includes the following inscription:
"Beneath this stone resteth the body of the Hon Ann Paston Daughter of the Rt Hon [[Charles Calvert, 3rd Baron Baltimore|Charles Calvert Baron Baltimore]] of the Kingdom of Ireland. She was wife to Edward Somerset of Pauntley Court in the County of Gloucestershire Esq. and after his death married John Paston of Horton Court in the said County Esq. She having punctually performed all the duties of a most loving wife, a tender mother, a faithful friend, in the care she took of her last husband's children by his first wife, her dear friend who lies interred by her, ended her life in a most tedious and painful sickness, suffered with the greatest courage and patience, on the 10th February MDCCXXXI (1731) ''cuius animae propitietur Deus''" ("To whose soul may God look on favourably").
Edward Somerset was fourth in descent from [[Edward Somerset, 4th Earl of Worcester]] (1553–1628) who had purchased Pauntley Court, near [[Newent]], Gloucestershire, from Sir Henry Poole of [[Sapperton, Gloucestershire]], whose family had inherited it by marriage to Eleanor Whittington, one of the five daughters of Thomas Whittington, eldest son of John Whittington (d.1525). John Paston had sometimes resided at Pauntley, which his second wife Anne Calvert must have held as her dower.See Glos. Archives Q/RNc/4/3 "Conveyance dated 1726 by John Paston of Pauntley, Esq., William Paston of Horton (probably his son, d. 1769) and William Nourse of Newent Esq.,..." Other monuments in the north aisle of the church to the Paston family include:[http://www.britishlistedbuildings.co.uk/en-34694-parish-church-of-st-james-the-elder-horto Parish Church of St James the Elder, Horton] *William Paston, died c. 1673, baroque, grey and white marbles, segmental pediment, winged cherubic heads, gadrooned base; *John Paston, died 1737 aged 67, grey and white marble, flat obelisk inscribed panel with gadrooned base, heraldry. He married as his second wife Anne Calvert (d.1731), whose monument has been described above. He had by his first wife a son Edward who died young in 1710,.Horton parish records, Glos. Notes & Queries He was probably the father of William Paston (see below).John Paston (1670-1737) and William Paston (1701-1769) made several joint conveyances, for example in 1730/1 of a lease in Horton to Jane Manning (Wilts. Archives 137/47) *William Paston, died 1769, by James Paty of Bristol, coloured and white marbles, gadrooned sarcophagus, heraldry and inscribed plinth. This is probably the son of John Paston (1670–1737) whose monument is listed above,Buried Horton 17/10/1737, aged 67: Horton parish records, Glos. Notes & Queries by his first wife Frances Tichborne (d.1712) who was buried at Horton. Sir George Throckmorton (1721–1767), only son of [[Sir Robert Throckmorton, 4th Baronet]] of [[Coughton Court]], Warwickshire, married Anna Maria Paston, daughter and sole heiress of William Paston (d.1769) of Horton by his wife Mary Courtenay (d.1747), the heiress of [[Manor of Molland|Molland]] in Devon. Anna Maria was also a co-heiress of [[Baron Arundell of Wardour|Thomas Arundell, 4th Baron Arundell of Wardour]] (1633–1712). ===Brooke=== [[File:Yate.stanshawes.court.arp.jpg|thumb|200px|Stanshaw's Court, Yate, Bristol]] The last of the Pastons mortgaged Horton Court to FitzHerbert Brooke, Esq., of Stanshaw's Court, [[Yate]], a solicitor, who foreclosed and became himself the proprietor of the manor soon after 1800. It was noted by [[Philip Bliss (academic)|Philip Bliss]] (1787–1857):[[Philip Bliss]], editor of Reliquiae Hearnianae, [https://archive.org/stream/gloucestershiren03londuoft/gloucestershiren03londuoft_djvu.txt Gloucestershire Notes & Queries, vol.3, 1887], p.161
"The last of the family lived at Horton, and becoming involved, fell into the hands of an attorney in the neighbourhood, to whom he ultimately became so indebted, that dying, he paid his debt by leaving the estate to this gentleman. There was, if I rightly remember, a suit at law in consequence, which, at the time, occasioned a great sensation in the County, and on the production of the Will, which (having been proved in some Consistory Court in the country, and erroneously sought for in the Prerogative Court in London only) was supposed not to exist, the cause was immediately decided in favour of the attorney."
The following mural tablet exists in the south transept of Old Sodbury Church:
"In memory of Fitzherbert Brooke of Stanshaw Court Esq. who died MDCCCXXV (1825) in the 49th year of his age. Also Theresa-Francis, relict of the above who died March 6th MDCCCXXX (1830) aged 51. And of their eldest son, Fitzherbert-Hartley who died in the 18th year of his age, November 15th 1830."
===Richards=== Horton Court passed to his grandson [[Frederick Richards|Sir Frederick Richards]] (1833–1912), [[Admiral of the Fleet]], who had married his daughter Lucy Fayle Brooke (d.1880), which marriage was without progeny. Richards made extensive alterations in 1884.Kingsley, p.111 ===Wills=== In 1937 Horton Court was purchased by Miss Hilda Proctor Wills (1880-13/5/1946), daughter of [[Wills baronets|Sir George Alfred Wills, 1st Bt of Blagdon]] (1854–1928) by his wife Susan Britton Proctor (1856–1904).{{Cite web |url=http://www.broadhurst-family.co.uk/FamilyTree/pafg18.htm |title=Broadhurst Family |access-date=9 January 2012 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304075832/http://www.broadhurst-family.co.uk/FamilyTree/pafg18.htm |url-status=live }} She was thus a member of the Bristol-based Wills family, proprietors of the [[Imperial Tobacco Company]] of Bristol. When she died in 1946, she left the property to the [[National Trust for Places of Historic Interest or Natural Beauty|National Trust]] in memory of her nephew [[Wills baronets|Sir George Peter Vernon Wills, 3rd Baronet of Blagdon]] (1922–1945), of the [[Coldstream Guards]], who had been killed in action in Italy.{{cite journal|title=Horton Court|journal=The Country Squire|first=Charles|last=Evans|date=4 July 2017}} === Filming === Horton Court has been used as a filming location in several television series including the BBC's [[Poldark (2015 TV series)|Poldark]], [[The Living and the Dead (TV series)|The Living and the Dead]]{{Cite web |title=The Living and the Dead: Where is Shepzoy House? |url=https://www.radiotimes.com/travel/the-living-and-the-dead-where-is-shepzoy-house/ |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=Radio Times |language=en |archive-date=11 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230511004828/https://www.radiotimes.com/travel/the-living-and-the-dead-where-is-shepzoy-house/ |url-status=live }} and [[Wolf Hall (TV series)|Wolf Hall]].{{Cite web |last=Hashish |first=Amira |date=2019-01-24 |title=Poldark manor house with Tudor walkway to rent for £5,250 a month |url=https://www.standard.co.uk/homesandproperty/celebrity-homes/rent-poldark-location-house-grade-ilisted-horton-court-in-bristol-used-in-several-bbc-shows-for-rent-a127376.html |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=Evening Standard |language=en |archive-date=11 May 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230511003327/https://www.standard.co.uk/homesandproperty/celebrity-homes/rent-poldark-location-house-grade-ilisted-horton-court-in-bristol-used-in-several-bbc-shows-for-rent-a127376.html |url-status=live }} ===National Trust=== It was listed in 1952. 6947742.title: Lodge Park and Sherborne Estate
6947742.extract:
Lodge Park was built as a grandstand in the Sherborne Estate near the villages of Sherborne, Aldsworth and Northleach in Gloucestershire, England.  The site is owned by the National Trust and the former grandstand is recorded in the National Heritage List for England as a designated Grade I listed building.  It is England's only surviving 17th-century deer course and grandstand.
In the 19th century Lodge Park was modified into a house, then a row of cottages, and then into a house again.  It was bequeathed to the National Trust in 1982, and restored to its original form as a grandstand.  Lodge Park is open to the public at advertised times, and the footpaths in the Sherborne Estate are available to the public at all times.

'''Lodge Park''' was built as a [[grandstand]] in the '''Sherborne Estate''' near the villages of [[Sherborne, Gloucestershire|Sherborne]], [[Aldsworth]] and [[Northleach]] in [[Gloucestershire]], England.  The site is owned by the [[National Trust]]<ref name="nt">{{Citation|title=Lodge Park and Sherborne Estate|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lodge-park-and-sherborne-estate|publisher=[[National Trust]]|access-date=11 September 2016}}</ref> and the former grandstand is recorded in the [[National Heritage List for England]] as a designated Grade I [[Listed building#England and Wales|listed building]].<ref name=images>{{NHLE |num= 1340791|desc= Lodge Park and adjoining walls and railings, Sherborne|accessdate= 20 August 2013|mode=cs2}}</ref>  It is England's only surviving 17th-century deer course and grandstand.<ref name=nt/><ref>{{Citation | year = 2010| title = National Trust Handbook: Lodge Park and Sherborne Estate| publisher = [[National Trust]]| page = 78}}</ref>

In the 19th century Lodge Park was modified into a house, then a row of cottages, and then into a house again.  It was bequeathed to the National Trust in 1982, and restored to its original form as a grandstand.  Lodge Park is open to the public at advertised times, and the footpaths in the Sherborne Estate are available to the public at all times.

==Lodge Park==

===History===

[[File:Lodge Park, view east down deer coursing enclosure.jpg|thumb|View east down the deer coursing enclosure]]

In the early 1630s John 'Crump' Dutton created a [[coursing|deer course]] on his Sherborne Estate; this consisted of a park for containing the deer, a mile-long walled enclosure for the chase, and, overlooking the finish, a grandstand.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=4.}}</ref>  His grandfather, Thomas Dutton, was descended from the Dutton family of [[Dutton, Cheshire|Dutton]], [[Cheshire]],<ref name=aslet>{{Citation | last = Aslet| first = Clive| author-link = Clive Aslet| date = 13 March 1986| title = Lodge Park, Gloucestershire| periodical = [[Country Life (magazine)|Country Life]] | publication-place = London| publisher = [[IPC Media]]}}</ref> and had bought the manor of Sherborne in 1551.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=27.}}</ref>  As originally constructed, the grandstand consisted of two storeys with a flat roof and a basement.  At the entrance was a [[portico]] with a balcony, and the basement contained the kitchens.  At the back of the building was a range containing the staircases linking the floors.  The ground floor was the entrance hall for welcoming guests, and the first floor consisted of the Great Room where the guests were entertained.  The deer coursing could be observed from the flat roof or from the balcony over the portico.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=6.}}</ref>
 
During the 1720s the building was remodelled and refurnished by [[Sir John Dutton, 2nd Baronet]].  New stone floors were added, a new plasterwork ceiling was added to the Great Room, and new furniture was designed.  Dutton employed [[Charles Bridgeman]] to redesign the landscaping. Jeffrey Haworth is of the opinion that the new interiors and some of the furniture was designed by [[William Kent]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=7, 28.}}</ref>

There were then few changes until the early 19th century when the building was modified to make it into a house.  The staircase range and the chimney piece from the Great Room were removed; the latter was incorporated in the rebuilding of [[Sherborne House, Gloucestershire|Sherborne House]] to the design of [[Lewis Wyatt]].  The removal of the staircase range adversely affected the stability of the house.  A [[pitched roof]] was installed in place of the original flat roof, lowering the ceiling of the former Great Room.  In the middle of the 19th century the interior of the building was gutted and it was converted into a row of cottages; this further impaired the stability of the building.<ref name=haw9>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=9.}}</ref>

Between 1898 and 1902 the building was converted into a [[dower house]] for Emily, the wife of [[Edward Dutton, 4th Baron Sherborne]].  The rear wing was rebuilt in a different form.  The first floor was made into a bedroom with an ''en suite'' bathroom.  The dining room was on the ground floor, with a lounge and a staircase in the newly built rear wing; the staircase led to a [[drawing room]] on the first floor.  However Lady Sherborne died in 1905 before her husband, and it is unlikely that she ever occupied the house.  Further alterations were made in 1938, when the house was tenanted, and again in the 1950s, when [[Charles Dutton, 7th Baron Sherborne]], and his wife moved into the house.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=9, 30.}}</ref>  Charles died in 1982 and bequeathed the house and the estate to the National Trust.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=31.}}</ref>

===Restoration===
When the National Trust acquired the property the house was in a poor condition; the external walls were moving and the chimney stacks were collapsing.<ref name=haw9/>  The interior consisted of "a jumble of small-scale modern rooms and corridors".<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=12.}}</ref>  [[Howard Colvin]] had discovered a 1634 description of the building. Further information was found in the Sherborne Archive in the [[Gloucestershire Archives|Gloucester Record Office]].  Essential repairs were carried out, and archaeological investigations revealed more evidence about the building's original form and its subsequent alterations.  It was decided to restore the building to a condition close to its original form.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=12–13.}}</ref>

===Architecture===

As [[Clive Aslet]] states, the building "is bursting with architecture".<ref name=aslet/>  A description written in 1634 suggests that the design was inspired by [[Inigo Jones]]' [[Banqueting House]] in [[Whitehall]], London.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=6–7.}}</ref> At one time it was thought that it had been designed by Jones, but this is incorrect.<ref name=aslet/>  The citation in ''[[Images of England]]'' states that it was probably designed by [[John Webb (architect)|John Webb]] and built by Valentine Strong of Taynton.<ref name=images/>

====Exterior====
The building is constructed in [[ashlar]] stone, with [[Rustication (architecture)|rusticate]]d [[Quoin (architecture)|quoin]]s and a [[Molding (decorative)|moulded]] [[plinth]]. Its main part has a rectangular plan in two storeys, with a flat lead roof and an extension to the rear. The east face forms the entrance front. It is symmetrical in five [[Bay (architecture)|bays]] with a protruding three-bay single-storey portico. The portico has three round arches on columns and is surmounted by a [[baluster|balustrade]]. The central doorway has a round arch and on each side are two [[mullion]]ed and [[Transom (architectural)|transomed]] windows. On the first floor is a central doorway with a mullioned window above and arched [[Niche (architecture)|niches]] in each side. The other bays contain mullioned and transomed windows. There are [[Course (architecture)#String course|string courses]] between the storeys and over the upper storey. Over the lateral two windows on the ground floor are curved [[Tympanum (architecture)|tympani]], and over each bay in the upper storey is a broken tympanum. Each of these tympani contains a sculpted human head. A balustrade runs around the top of the roof, and at its rear are six joined chimneys.<ref name=images/><ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=14–15.}}</ref>

====Interior====
[[File:Lodge Park, great room interior.jpg|thumb|Great Room interior]]
The entrance hall contains two original arches.  One of these includes a fireplace, the other leads to the staircase.  The National Trust has inserted a [[Panelling|panelled]] wall on the left.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=15.}}</ref> The staircase has been rebuilt by the National Trust in a [[Stairway|stairwell]] measuring {{convert|18|ft|m|0}} by {{convert|18|ft|m|0}}, and its oak [[baluster]]s have been copied from those at [[Cornbury Park]] in [[Oxfordshire]].<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|pp=17–18.}}</ref>

The Great Room on the first floor has been restored in an attempt to link with its original design, including its classical ordering with a [[Dado (architecture)|dado]], [[pilaster]]s and [[entablature]].  The walls would have been hung with [[tapestry]], but this has been replaced with family portraits that originally hung in Sherborne House.  The floor has been reconstructed, using [[chestnut]] boards measuring {{convert|49|ft|m|0}} from the Welsh borders.  The chimneypiece has been reconstructed by masons from the [[Hereford Cathedral]] workshop.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=19.}}</ref>

===Associated structures===

Three structures associated with the Lodge Park have been designated as Grade II listed buildings by [[Historic England]].  About {{convert|10|m|ft|0}} to the south of building is a pair of gates with [[Pier (architecture)|piers]] that date from the mid-18th century or earlier.  The gates are constructed in [[cast iron]] and the piers are in [[limestone]].  The piers consist of hammer-dressed quoins up to the level of the top of the gates; on the top of each is a large stone block surmounted by a triangular pedimented capping stone.<ref>{{NHLE |num= 1090486|desc= Gate piers and gates c10m south of Lodge Park, Sherborne|accessdate= 20 August 2013|mode=cs2|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>  Some {{convert|40|m|ft|0}} to the east is a fountain probably dating from 1898.  This consists of a circular stone surround with four [[urn]]s, one at each [[Cardinal direction|cardinal point]].  In the centre is the fountain, also in the form of an urn, but larger than those on the surround.<ref>{{NHLE |num= 1155866|desc= Fountain to the east of Lodge Park, Sherborne|accessdate= 20 August 2013|mode=cs2|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>  Further to the east, some {{convert|120|m|ft|0}} from the building, is a pair of limestone lodges with adjoining walls, gate piers and gates also dating from about 1898.<ref>{{NHLE |num= 1090431|desc= Pair of lodges and adjoining walls and gates and gatepiers to the east of Lodge Park, Sherborne|accessdate= 20 August 2013|mode=cs2|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

===Parkland===

To the west of Park Lodge is an area of parkland of 115 hectares.  This was landscaped to a design by [[Charles Bridgeman]] from the mid-1720s for Sir John Dutton.<ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=5.}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | url = http://www.parksandgardens.ac.uk/component/option,com_parksandgardens/task,site/id,2136/tab,summary/Itemid,292/ | title = Lodge Park, Aldsworth, Cheltenham, England | access-date = 8 June 2010 | publisher = Parks & Gardens Data Services}}</ref>  It is registered by [[Historic England]] as Grade I.<ref>{{NHLE |num= 1000770|desc= Lodge Park, Sherborne|accessdate= 20 August 2013|mode=cs2|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>  The park contained a series of "rooms" (presumably for herding deer), a Great Avenue, and a former canal. Bridgeman's proposal for a [[Serpentine shape|serpentine]] canal <ref>{{Harvnb|Haworth|2002|p=26.}}</ref> was not carried through.

In the parkland there is a [[long barrow]] at map reference SP1426712550, with a capstone and two upright stones visible at the south-eastern end.<ref>{{Citation | url=http://www.megalithic.co.uk/article.php?sid=7802 | title=Lodge Park Long Barrow | year=2004 | work=The Megalithic Portal | access-date=7 April 2013}}</ref>

==Sherborne Estate==
The estate is open to the public.  It contains wild animals including fallow and roe deer, badgers and foxes.  There are a number of footpaths and walks in the estate, including a sculpture trail; some of these start from Ewe Pen Barn ({{gbmapping|SP158143}}).  On the estate are [[water-meadow]]s, including draining channels and [[sluice]]s ({{gbmapping|SP175154}}).<ref name=nt/>

The estate was the venue for the [[BBC Two]] wildlife television programmes ''[[Springwatch]]'' and ''Autumnwatch'' in 2017,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lodge-park-and-sherborne-estate/news/springwatch-comes-to-sherborne|title=Springwatch comes to Sherborne Park|date=30 May 2017|website=National Trust|language=en|access-date=9 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/lodge-park-and-sherborne-estate/autumnwatch|title=Autumnwatch at Lodge Park and Sherborne Estate|date=October 2017|website=National Trust|language=en|access-date=9 November 2017}}</ref> followed by ''Winterwatch'' in January 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b09qmn6p|title = BBC Two - Winterwatch, Series 6}}</ref>

==Present day==
Lodge Park is open to the public at advertised times and has a small shop and provides light refreshments.  The building is available for weddings.  The Sherborne Estate is open all year.<ref name=nt/>

'''Newark Park''' is a [[Listed building|Grade I listed]]<ref name="NHLE">{{National Heritage List for England| num=1227685 |desc=Newark Park |grade=I |accessdate=28 October 2015}}</ref> [[country house]] of [[Tudor style architecture|Tudor]] origins located near the village of [[Ozleworth]], [[Wotton-under-Edge]], [[Gloucestershire]], England. The house sits in an estate of {{convert|700|acres|km2}}<ref name='NT'>{{cite book | last = Claydon | first = Michael | title = Newark Park | publisher = National Trust | year = 2002 }}</ref> at the southern end of the [[Cotswold]] [[escarpment]] with views down the [[Severn Valley]] to the [[River Severn|Severn Estuary]].<ref name=Greeves/> The house and estate have been in the care of the [[National Trust]] since 1946.

[[File:Basement kitchen at Newark Park.jpg|thumb|Basement kitchen at Newark Park]]

== History ==
Newark Park was originally a four-[[storey]] (three storeys over a basement) [[Tudor period|Tudor]] [[Hunting and shooting in the United Kingdom#Hunting lodge|hunting lodge]] built between 1544 and 1556<ref name='NT'/> for Sir [[Nicholas Poyntz]] (d.1557), whose main seat was at [[Acton Court]] near [[Bristol]], some fifteen miles to the south, an easy day's ride. The Poyntz family were anciently [[Feudal barony of Curry Mallet|feudal barons of Curry Mallet]] in [[Somerset]], later of [[Manor of Iron Acton|Iron Acton]] in [[Gloucestershire]]. Poyntz was a [[Groom of the Privy Chamber]] to [[Henry VIII]]<ref name='Greeves'>{{cite book | last = Greeves | first = Linda | title = History and Landscape | publisher = National Trust Books | year = 2006 | pages = 261 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=VY-GweXXNO0C&dq=%22newark+park%22&pg=PA261| isbn = 978-1-905400-13-3}}</ref> and had recently remodeled Acton Park in anticipation of a royal visit. "Newark is equally fashionable in terms of its precocious classicism," observes Nicholas Cooper, who points out its rigorously symmetrical front (''illustration''), unprecedented in the main body of any great house in its time, and the correct [[Tuscan order]] of its original main door.<ref>Now a side entrance. Nicholas Cooper, ''English Houses of the Gentry, 1480–1680'' (Yale University Press) 1999:112.</ref> The house was then called "New Work"<ref name='NT'/> and was partly constructed with building materials from the recently [[Dissolution of the Monasteries|dissolved]] [[Kingswood Abbey]],<ref name=Greeves/> some five miles away. The lodge was three bays wide and of single-pile construction, one room deep. In the basement was a kitchen, there were two reception rooms on the ground floor and a banqueting room on the first.<ref name='Gomme'>{{cite book | last = Gomme | first = Andor |author2=Maguire, Alison  | title = Design and Design and Plan in the Country House: From Castle Donjons to Palladian Boxes | publisher = Yale University Press | year = 2008 | pages = 56–57 | isbn = 978-0-300-12645-7 }}</ref> Modest sleeping quarters were provided on the third floor, and the roof was flat so that it could be used as a pleasurable lookout over the surrounding countryside,<ref name='NT'/> in which it enjoys a commanding position. It was built at about the same time as nearby [[Siston Court]] was being built by [[Sir Maurice Denys]] (d.1563), first cousin of Poyntz's wife Jane Berkeley. Poyntz's original lodge now forms the eastern part of the present structure.

In 1600 the lodge was sold to the Low family of [[London]] who in 1672 significantly extended the building by the addition of a second four-storey building to the west, which was joined to the original by a passage [[stairway]] creating an H-shaped footprint. The Lows owned Newark Park until 1722 when it was sold for £6,010 (equivalent to £{{formatnum:{{Inflation|UK|6010|1722|r=-3}}}} today) to the Harding family who after making some minor alterations sold it to James Clutterbuck. The Clutterbucks engaged the architect [[James Wyatt]] to remodel it into a four-square house in 1790. Their improvements included the creation of a formal deer-park to the south of the house and landscaping of the rest of the grounds.

The Clutterbucks left Newark in 1860 and let it out, but even though it was [[Leasehold estate|tenanted]] the occupants continued to make alterations and improvements. Mrs Annie Poole King, [[widow]] of a [[Bristol]] [[Ship transport|shipping merchant]] took the leasehold in 1898, moving from the larger [[Standish House]] at [[Stonehouse, Gloucestershire]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.stonehousehistorygroup.org.uk/page54.html|title=Stadish House|publisher=Stonehouse History Group|access-date=2012-02-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140621115535/http://stonehousehistorygroup.org.uk/page54.html|archive-date=2014-06-21|url-status=dead}}</ref> A member of the [[Berkeley Hunt]], she had five children, plus a house staff of a coachman, cook, housekeeper, and gardener. The King family added [[servants' quarters]] on the north side, installed a [[Central heating|hot-air heating system]] and ran [[hot water]] to the second floor. The Kings stayed at Newark until 1949 when the last of the line died and the then owner, Mrs Power-Clutterbuck, gave Newark Park and its estates to the National Trust.<ref name='NT'/>

== Conservation and listing ==
When the Trust took ownership they did not open Newark Park to the public but instead let it out to tenants who ran it as a [[nursing home]]. By 1970 the house was in a state of disrepair and the gardens overgrown. It was in this state that [[United States|American]] [[Architecture|architect]] Robert (Bob) Parsons (1920–2000), who had long expressed a desire to take on an English country house in need of repair, took the tenancy and began a painstaking programme of [[renovation]], [[Conservation-restoration|conservation]] and rehabilitation to both the house and the grounds.<ref>Parsons' restoration was described and illustrated by Richard Haslam, "Newark Park, Gloucestershire", ''Country Life,'' CLXXXVIII (1985), pp 943–47.</ref> It was due to Bob Parson's efforts that the architectural importance of the house was acknowledged and the Grade I listing achieved.<ref name="NT" />  Parson's partner, Michael Claydon, moved to Newark Park in 1982 and became actively involved in the ongoing restoration.  After Parson's death in 2000, Claydon maintained stewardship of the house and continued restoration works in the landscaped parkland.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2010-02-24|title=The Restoration of Newark Park – Old House Journal Magazine|url=https://www.oldhouseonline.com/house-tours/the-restoration-of-newark-park/|access-date=2021-08-29|website=Old House Journal Magazine|language=en-us}}</ref>

==Public Access==
The property is now open to the public in summer every day and weekends in winter.<ref>{{cite web |title=Newark Park, visitor information |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/gloucestershire-cotswolds/newark-park |website=National Trust |access-date=4 September 2025}}</ref>

16899240.extract: Westbury Court Garden is a Dutch water garden in Westbury-on-Severn, Gloucestershire, England, 9 miles (14 km) southwest of Gloucester. It is a rare survival of seventeenth century garden design and was initially laid out by the owner of Westbury Court, Maynard Colchester I,  in 1696–1705. The garden has been under the guardianship of the National Trust since 1967.

'''Westbury Court Garden''' is a [[Dutch garden|Dutch]] [[water garden]] in [[Westbury-on-Severn]], [[Gloucestershire]], [[England]], {{convert|9|mi|km}} southwest of [[Gloucester]]. It is a rare survival of seventeenth century garden design and was initially laid out by the owner of Westbury Court, Maynard Colchester I,  in 1696–1705. The garden has been under the guardianship of the [[National Trust]] since 1967.

== Background ==
The garden was laid out in 1696–1705,<ref>Irvine Gray, "The Making of Westbury Court Gardens" (Garden History Society Occasional Paper No. 1 (1969:15–18).</ref> a rare survival<ref>Other contemporary gardens characterised as "Dutch" rather than "French" by John D. Hunt (''The Anglo-Dutch Garden in the Age of William and Mary'') were the topiary garden of Winchenden House, Buckinghamshire, and [[Hartwell, Buckinghamshire|Hartwell]] (known only through engravings).</ref> not to have been replaced in the 18th century by a naturalistic garden landscape as popularised by [[Capability Brown]].<ref name="Greeves">{{cite book |last=Greeves |first=Linda |title=History and Landscape |publisher=National Trust Books |year=2006 |page=423 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VY-GweXXNO0C&dq=%22westbury+court%22++canal&pg=PA423 |isbn=978-1-905400-13-3}}</ref> It is situated facing the high street of the rural village, extending on low-lying water meadows adjacent to the [[River Severn]]; the flat watery ground makes the site well suited to a [[Dutch garden|Dutch-style garden]], of which Westbury is the outstanding survival in Britain.  [[Christopher Hussey (historian)|Christopher Hussey]] associated the Dutch style not so much with [[topiary]] as with canals, giving Westbury Court as the prime example, observes [[David Jacques]].<ref>"Who Knows What a Dutch Garden Is?" ''Garden History'' '''30'''.2, Dutch Influences (Winter 2002:114–130) p. 123.</ref>  Similarly [[Miles Hadfield]] considered that "an essential of Dutch versions of the grand manner was that the ground be tolerably level, with an abundance of water".<ref>Hadfield, ''Gardening in Britain'' 1960:154.</ref> Later, Hadfield found "not the slightest hint" of a Dutch connection at Westbury Court,<ref>Hadfield, "William, Mary, and Westbury", ''Garden History'' '''2''' (1974:27–33).</ref> overlooking Maynard Colchester's close friendship with [[Catharina Boevey]] of [[Flaxley Abbey]].<ref name=Gray16/>

== Layout ==
The garden's centrepiece is a {{convert|137|m|ft}} long [[canal (garden history)|canal]] (''illustration, right''), centred on a two-storey [[Dutch Golden Age|Dutch style]] red-brick [[pavilion]] at one end and a large [[wrought iron]] gate in the wall at the far end, designed to extend the vista from the pavilion out into the surrounding countryside. The main canal is flanked by [[Taxus baccata|yew]] and [[holly]] [[topiary]] in pyramids and balls. A second red-brick building, a [[summer house]] built in 1702–04, overlooks a T-shaped canal running parallel to the main canal. Behind the summer house is a small walled garden of cottage plants and beyond the water garden is an orchard of fruit trees, which also contains an ancient [[Live oak|evergreen oak]] planted in the 17th century, the largest ever recorded,<ref name="Strong">{{cite book |last=Strong |first=Roy |author-link=Roy Strong |author2=Oman, Julia Trevelyan |title=Garden Party: collected Writings, 1979–1999 |publisher=[[Frances Lincoln Publishers]] |year=2000 |pages=104 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9szIOBU0dMYC&dq=%22westbury+court%22+oak&pg=PA104 |isbn=978-0-7112-1458-3}}</ref> it is also claimed to be the oldest in [[England]].<ref name=Greeves/>

== History ==
[[File:Westbury Court Gardens in Gloucestershire.jpg|thumb|Westbury Court ''[[parterre]]s'' and the pavilion.]]
The garden at Westbury was created by the owner of Westbury Court, Maynard Colchester I, between 1697, when the brook was first diverted, and 1705. Impetus may have been provided by the canal garden nearby at Flaxley Abbey,<ref>"A handsome house and pleasant garden" according to Atkyns (quoted in Gray 1969:16).</ref> which was the seat of Colchester's close friend Catharina Boevey, the widow of William Boevey, member of a Dutch merchant family settled at London; Kip's engraving of Flaxley shows a long rectangular canal, of which only traces remain.<ref name=Gray16>Gray 1969: 16</ref> Clipped accents to set off the pyramidal yews were provided by 'headed' [[Laurustinus]], headed and pyramidal [[Phillyrea]] and "[[Daphne mezereum|Mizerean trees]]" in sixes and pairs.<ref>Noted from the account book by Gray 1969. For ''[[Daphne mezereum]]'' compare the advice of Timothy Nourse (died 1699), printed in John Dixon Hunt and Peter Willis, ''The Genius of the Place: The English Landscape Garden 1620–1820'' (1975) 1988:103: "Let there be planted likewise up and down some little Tufts or Matts of Peaks for these look prettily in the Winter, as also some Mizerean Trees and the like."</ref>

Colchester died in 1715, and the garden continued to be developed by his nephew and heir, Maynard Colchester II, who was probably responsible for the summerhouse and the small walled garden.<ref name="Goulty">{{cite book |last=Goulty |first=Sheena |title=Heritage Gardens |publisher=[[Routledge]] |year=1993 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/heritagegardensc0000goul/page/18 18]–19 |url=https://archive.org/details/heritagegardensc0000goul |url-access=registration |isbn=978-0-415-07474-2}}</ref>

Maynard Colchester II also demolished the original late [[Elizabethan architecture|Elizabethan]] [[manor house]] of Westbury Court<ref>The Elizabethan Westbury Court was built for the Baynham family (Gray 1969).</ref> in the 1740s and built a [[Palladian architecture|Palladian]] mansion in its stead, to designs of a little-known mason of [[Bristol]], Michael Sidnell.<ref>[[Howard Colvin]], ''A Biographical Dictionary of British Architects, 1600–1840'', 3rd ed. ([[Yale University Press]]) 1995, ''s.v.'' "Sidnell, Michael". Payments 1742–45 are recorded in the account book formerly in possession of a Colchester descendant, Sir Francis Colchester-Wemyss, now at the Gloucestershire Record Office.</ref> This was in turn replaced by a 19th-century [[country house]], no longer standing.

== Johannes Kip engraving ==
[[File:Westbury Court Garden Kip.jpg|left|thumb|[[Johannes Kip]]'s 1712 engraving of the house and gardens.]]In 1707, a birds-eye view of the Westbury Court and its garden was engraved by [[Johannes Kip]] for his ''Britannia Illustrata: Or Views of Several of the Queens Palaces, as Also of the Principal seats of the Nobility and Gentry of Great Britain, Curiously Engraven on 80 Copper Plates''; it shows the main canal, topiary, parterres and the pavilion.<ref name="Elliot">{{cite book |last=Elliot |first=Charles |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=V2Qc1EsgDLwC&dq=%22westbury+court%22++canal&pg=PA176 |title=The Transplanted Gardener |publisher=Frances Lincoln Publishers |year=2004 |isbn=978-0-7112-2380-6 |pages=176}}</ref> The cross-axis canal was a later addition, which is not shown, it does appear in a later Kip engraving published in 1712 in [[Robert Atkyns (topographer)|Robert Atkyns]]' ''The Ancient and Present State of Gloucester''.

== Restoration ==
By 1967, with the manor house gone and the garden derelict, the [[National Trust]] — who had never been responsible for a garden restoration before — accepted the care of Westbury Court Garden.<ref name=Stuart/> [[Miles Hadfield]], then president of the [[Garden history|Garden History Society]], was influential in persuading the Trust to do so.<ref name=Stuart/> In 1971, work started on the restoration with aid of Colchester's meticulous accounts, Kip's engravings and the evidence on the ground. Authenticity was paramount: in the water garden only plants introduced before 1700 were used,<ref name="Stuart">{{cite book |last=Thomas |first=Graham Stuart |title=Recollections of Great Gardeners |publisher=Frances Lincoln Publishers |year=2003 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/recollectionsofg0000thom/page/27 27] |url=https://archive.org/details/recollectionsofg0000thom |url-access=registration |isbn=978-0-7112-2288-5}}</ref> though the appearance aimed at was the maturing garden in about 1720.<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/westbury-court-garden/features/history National Trust "History" page]</ref>

The gardens are Grade II* listed on the [[Register of Historic Parks and Gardens of special historic interest in England|Register of Historic Parks and Gardens]].<ref name=NHLE>{{NHLE|num=1000786|desc=Westbury Court|access-date=21 September 2016|mode=cs2}}</ref>

36915612.title: Minchinhampton Common
36915612.extract:
Minchinhampton Common (grid reference SO855010) is a 182.7-hectare (451-acre) biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest in Minchinhampton, Gloucestershire, England, notified in 1972.
The common has been owned and managed by the National Trust since 1913. It is one of the largest grassland commons in the Cotswold area.  It is south of Rodborough Common SSSI.  Both commons are on Jurassic limestone and are a central plateau with steep sides. They drop down to the Nailsworth Valley on the west side and the Frome Valley on the north side.  The site designation includes the outlying areas of Iron Mills and Littleworth Commons. Neu-Lindsey Nature Reserve adjoins the western edge of Minchinhampton Common.
Minchinhampton Common is of both geological and biological importance.  There are disused quarries near the centre which provide fossil evidence for research purposes.  It is unimproved, herb-rich grassland. There are five units of assessment.
The limestone Longstone of Minchinhampton is supposedly the burial site of a Danish leader, and the area on the east side of the common known as Woefuldane Bottom has been suggested as a possible site of the Battle of Edington.
The Old Lodge, a former hunting lodge, stands at the centre of the common.

'''Minchinhampton Common''' ({{gbmapping|SO855010}}) is a {{convert|182.7  |ha|adj=on}} [[biological and geological Site of Special Scientific Interest]] in [[Minchinhampton]], [[Gloucestershire]], England, [[SSSI notification|notified]] in 1972.<ref name="NE citation">[http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/Special/sssi/sssi_details.cfm?sssi_id=1002432 Natural England SSSI information on the citation]</ref><ref>[http://www.stroud.gov.uk/docs/planning/planning_strategy.asp#s=sectioncontent1 Stroud District Local Plan, adopted November 2005, Appendix 6 ‘Sites of Nature Conservation Interest’] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120606002516/http://www.stroud.gov.uk/docs/planning/planning_strategy.asp |date=2012-06-06 }}</ref>

The common has been owned and managed by the [[National Trust of England|National Trust]] since 1913.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-10 |title=Warning: Cows coming out {{!}} Stroud Times |url=https://stroudtimes.com/warning-cows-coming-out/ |access-date=2024-07-15 |language=en-GB}}</ref> It is one of the largest grassland commons in the [[Cotswold]] area.  It is south of [[Rodborough Common]] SSSI.  Both commons are on [[Jurassic]] [[limestone]] and are a central plateau with steep sides. They drop down to the [[Nailsworth]] Valley on the west side and the [[Frome]] Valley on the north side.  The site designation includes the outlying areas of Iron Mills and Littleworth Commons.<ref name="NE citation"/> [[Neu-Lindsey Nature Reserve]] adjoins the western edge of Minchinhampton Common.<ref>Kelham, A, Sanderson, J, Doe, J, Edgeley-Smith, M, ''et al.'', 1979, 1990, 2002 editions, 'Nature Reserves of the Gloucestershire Trust for Nature Conservation/Gloucestershire Wildlife Trust'</ref>

Minchinhampton Common is of both geological and biological importance.  There are disused quarries near the centre which provide fossil evidence for research purposes.  It is unimproved, ''herb-rich'' grassland.<ref name="NE citation"/> There are five units of assessment.<ref>[http://www.sssi.naturalengland.org.uk/Special/sssi/unitlist.cfm?sssi_id=1002432 Natural England SSSI information on the Minchinhampton units]</ref>

The limestone [[Longstone of Minchinhampton]] is supposedly the burial site of a [[Denmark|Danish]] leader,<ref name=menhir>{{cite journal|last1=Partridge|first1=J. B.|title=Cotswold Place-Lore and Customs|journal=Folklore|date=1912|volume=23|issue=3|pages=339–341|jstor=1255154}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Darvill|first1=Timothy|title=Prehistoric Gloucestershire: Forests and Vales and High Blue|date=2013|publisher=Amberley Publishing Limited|isbn=9781445619941|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bWqoAwAAQBAJ}}</ref> and the area on the east side of the common known as Woefuldane Bottom has been suggested as a possible site of the [[Battle of Edington]].<ref>J.M.Moffat. [https://books.google.com/books?id=aY8MAAAAYAAJ&q=106&pg=PA106 Battle of Ethandun] pp. 106 – 110 ''in'' Brayley. The graphic and Historical Illustrator. via Google Books Retrieved 4 March 2012</ref>

[[The Old Lodge (Minchinhampton)|The Old Lodge]], a former [[Hunting and shooting in the United Kingdom|hunting lodge]], stands at the centre of the common.

== History ==
There was a wood on the Common during the 1300s.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Short |first=Christopher J. |url=https://eprints.glos.ac.uk/10758/ |title=7th National Seminar on Common Land and Town and Village Greens (2007) |date=2007-09-11 |publisher=CCRI, University of Gloucestershire |location=Cheltenham |language=en}}</ref>

In 1739, Anglican preacher, [[George Whitefield]] delivered a sermon to 30,000 people. The Neolithic burial mound on the Common is known as ''Whitfield's Tump'' was named after him.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bowden |first=Mark |title=An Archaeology of Town Commons in England: "A Very Fair Field Indeed" |last2=Brown |first2=Graham |last3=Smith |first3=Nicky |publisher=[[English Heritage]] |year=2009 |isbn=9781848020351}}</ref>

Those who own property within Minchinhampton Manor today, still have [[grazing rights]] on the Common,<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Minchinhampton & Rodborough Commons |url=https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/visit/gloucestershire-cotswolds/minchinhampton-and-rodborough-commons/explore-minchinhampton-and-rodborough-commons |access-date=2024-06-21 |website=National Trust |language=en}}</ref> as was custom in the [[open-field system]] before [[enclosure]].

==Geology==
The quarries are one of the most important Bathonian (Middle Jurassic) research sites in the [[United Kingdom]]. The fossil Limestones provide examples of various marine species including [[bivalve]] and [[gastropod]] fauna including [[limpet]]s and thick-shelled [[sea snail]]s, [[coral]], [[crustacea]]ns, and [[reptile]]s. The site provides opportunities for significant further research on the local rock strata of the Minchinhampton and Burleigh limestones, and the relationship to the Bathonian successions to the east and south.<ref name="NE citation"/>

==Biology==

===Flora===
The central plateau supports a short grassland sward (due to stock grazing) with longer vegetation on the steeper slopes. The grassland includes [[upright brome]], [[tor-grass]], [[sheep's fescue]], [[quaking grass]], and [[crested dog's-tail]]. Flowering herbs include [[common rock-rose]], [[harebell]], [[Polygala|chalk milkwort]], and [[field scabious]].  The area has a significant population of orchids, including the [[Ophrys apifera|bee orchid]], [[fragrant orchid]], and [[frog orchid]].<ref name="NE citation"/>

There are more neutral grasslands and herb species in areas of landslip on the margins of the site. There are wet areas which support [[marsh]]y vegetation. There are also areas of scrub which is dominated by [[Crataegus|hawthorn]], [[bramble]], and [[dog rose]]. There is [[juniper]] on the site and a limited amount of broad-leaved woodland on the margins.<ref name="NE citation"/>

===Fauna===
The site is known for its variety of invertebrates and butterflies recorded are [[chalkhill blue]], [[small blue]], [[marsh fritillary]] and [[Duke of Burgundy fritillary]]. Moth records include [[cistus forester]] and [[juniper carpet]].<ref name="NE citation"/>

The rare [[greater horseshoe bat]] is recorded as hibernating in the disused stone mines on the Nailsworth side.<ref name="NE citation"/>

===Usage===
There is a golf club and course.<ref>[http://minchinhamptongolfclub.co.uk/ Minchinhampton Golf Club]</ref> The grass is used to graze cattle in the warmer months, this is administered by the "hayward".<ref>[https://www.nationaltrust.org.uk/minchinhampton-and-rodborough-commons/documents/get-a-copy-of-the-pink-helpful-handbook-here.pdf National Trust PDF page 16 (hayward)]</ref> Because of the cattle roaming free, there is a speed limit of 40 mph in the area. Part of the common was used to house a US military field hospital<ref>[https://www.airfieldresearchgroup.org.uk/forum/war-office-and-army-units/3813-army-camps-barracks-gloucestershire Army Camps & Barracks in Gloucestershire]</ref> during WW2.

Castlefield Viaduct is a 330-metre (1,080 ft) long former railway viaduct built in 1893, which used to carry heavy rail traffic in and out of the Great Northern Warehouse, located in the Castlefield area of Manchester, England.
The Grade II listed viaduct was designed by Heenan & Froude, the same engineering company behind Blackpool Tower. The viaduct is part of the Historical Railways Estate and since 2022 approximately a third of its length is a sky park.
